newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury eyes use of SLGS as a hedge sometimes.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury eyes use of SLGS as a hedge sometimes.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury Department is exploring whether to let bond firms use State and Local Government Series securities (SLGS) as an interest rate hedge if the federal government is compensated for the option, an industry representative said Wednesday.

Amy Dunbar, head of governmental affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, said Treasury officials informally have requested input from municipal industry groups on how dealers could pay the federal government for the use of the option.
Sources said PSA The Bond Market Trade Association responded in a letter to Treasury at the beginning of the week. PSA, however, did not release a copy of a letter.
Roger Anderson, deputy assistant secretary for federal finance at Treasury, was traveling and unavailable for comment.
The debate stems from a letter that PSA, NABL and seven other groups sent to Anderson on April 28 warning of a loophole in final SLGS regulations issued by Treasury last October.
Treasury's new rules are designed to make the SLGS program easier and less costly for state and local governments that want to refinance and invest proceeds from tax-exempt bonds.

But the groups warned that the new SLGS rules reduce significantly the time periods for subscribing to and cancelling SLGS orders and eliminate a requirement that SLGS cancellations can be based on "cause."

They warned that as a result, there is no penalty attached to subscribing for SLGS up to 60 days prior to delivery and then canceling the subscription within five to seven of the the scheduled delivery date.
"This allows the SLGS program to be used to create an 'option' or 'hedge' on interest rates, with no penalty to the SLGS subscriber," the letter to Treasury said.
Dunbar said on Wednesday that NABL has no problem with the idea of paying the government for the use of the option.

"Certainly, the Treasury is figuring out how to be most responsive to issuers' needs in the SLGS program," Dunbar said. "That would be one further level of flexibility that they would be offering," she said, referring to the payment option.
